1.definition: Hans Robert Roemer (1915-1997) was a German orientalist and historian, a leading twentieth-century scholar of late-medieval and early-modern Iran — the Timurids, the Turkmen confederations, and the Safavids. He wrote the influential 'Safavid Period' and 'Timur in Iran' chapters of The Cambridge History of Iran, and is cited here for his characterization of early Qizilbash religion as closer to a millenarian cult than to orthodox Shia Islam.

2.definition: Yavuz ("the Grim" or "the Resolute") is the Ottoman honorific by which Sultan Selim I is remembered — a tribute to the ruthless decisiveness with which he eliminated rivals, crushed the Safavids at Chaldiran in 1514, and conquered the Mamluk Sultanate to make the Ottomans the dominant Muslim power.

3.definition: One of the most influential Persian painters of any era, a leading master of the Tabriz school whose full-page miniatures filled the great illustrated manuscripts produced for the Safavid court.

The poetic pen name under which Shah Ismail I wrote his verse — mostly in Turkic, some in Persian. Like other Persian and Turkic poets he adopted a takhallus (a single signature word woven into his closing lines), and his collected poems circulated as the Divan-i Khata'i. The melancholy verse he produced after Chaldiran was written under this name.

The two-century entanglement between Safavid Iran and Mughal India, defined by a mix of cultural intimacy and political rivalry. The two courts shared the Persian language and a common high culture of poetry, painting, and manners, and exchanged artists, scholars, and refugees freely; at the same time they fought repeatedly over the strategic frontier city of Kandahar, which changed hands several times between them.

4.definition: A Persian tile technique whose name means "seven colors": several glaze colors were painted onto large tile panels and fired together, instead of cutting and assembling tiny single-color mosaic pieces. Faster to make, and stunning on a building.

4.term: Classical Age of the Ottoman Empire

5.definition: A small village near Qom in central Iran. It is remembered almost entirely as the place of Mulla Sadra's rural exile, where, cut off from the patronage and the persecution of Isfahan, he wrote the bulk of his major philosophical work over roughly seven to twelve years.

Arabic for "reports" or "traditions" — the transmitted narrations attributed to the Prophet and the Twelve Imams. The Akhbari school of Shia jurisprudence took its name from these reports, holding that religious guidance should come from applying them as directly as possible, with no independent reasoning by the contemporary scholar.

8.definition: The institutionally independent clerical class the Safavids created to staff their new Twelver Shia state — Iranian-trained mujtahids who, by the late Safavid period, had grown powerful enough to set religious policy themselves. When Nader Shah tried to fold Shia Islam back into Sunnism in 1736, this clergy simply refused, demonstrating that it had outgrown the dynasty that built it. That same clerical establishment is the direct ancestor of the marja-i taqlid system and, ultimately, the clerical leadership of the modern Islamic Republic.
